text: Pella, 336 BC. Philip lies murdered at his own wedding games, and the phalanx roars your name — a twenty-year-old king with a doctrine of the spear and a copy of the Iliad under his pillow. The empire of Persia waits across the sea; but first, Macedonia must answer to you.

choices.text: Secure the north first — Thrace and Illyria before Asia
Cross the Hellespont at once — Asia waits for no one

text: The Triballi break at Mount Haemus and the Illyrian war-bands scatter into their hills. At the Danube, Scythian riders shadow your camp by night, counting fires, weighing your youth.

choices.text: Crush the Triballi root and branch — let the north learn the price of defiance
Turn the Scythian clans with silver and oaths of friendship

text: The River Granicus runs fast and shallow in the spring melt. On the far bank, Memnon of Rhodes waits with the Persian cavalry, spears glinting. Parmenion counsels camp and dawn; the afternoon sun will be in their eyes — and yours.

choices.text: Charge the far bank at the head of the Companions — now, while they wait for parley
Send the phalanx across in column and grind the bank flat
Withdraw and recross another day — the king who hurries meets his ferryman early

text: Issus, 333 BC. You have stolen behind him. Darius himself waits in the center of the Great Line, his household behind it — his mother, his wife, his children. The Persian host is wider than a city and deeper than a phalanx is long.

choices.text: Anchor the left and break the center where the Great King stands
Refuse the field; take the coastal cities and their harbors instead

text: Tyre: an island fortress with the best fleet in the world and walls grown from the sea. They offered you token submission and forbade you their temple — an old city's arithmetic of pride. The mole you mean to build will take months and forests.

choices.text: Build the mole — join island to shore and make the sea itself your road
Spare the siege — let Tyre's fleet sail under your banner instead

text: Egypt receives you as a liberator and a pharaoh without a fight. Memphis feasts you; the priests of Ptah know a son of Ammon when they see one coming. West of the Delta lies a fishing village where a harbor dreams of being the hinge of the world.

choices.text: Cross the desert to the oracle of Ammon at Siwa
Stay on the coast and found Alexandria between the marsh and the sea

text: Gaugamela, 331 BC. Darius has had two years to choose his ground, and he has chosen well: a plain wide enough for scythed chariots and elephants, leveled for his wheeling horse. His engineers even removed the humps. Tonight his torches outnumber the stars.

choices.text: Anchor the line, refuse both wings, and punch through the Great King's guard
Bribe the eastern satraps until the Great King's flanks melt away
Shadow the Persian host, cut its supply, and let the plain starve first

text: The left wing folds before your wedge even touches the guard. Parmenion's messengers arrive three times too late; the phalanx breaks on the chariot lanes Darius leveled for exactly this. The expedition survives — barely — and retreats to the coast. In Macedon, they will call it Philip's war, not yours.

Persepolis, the staircased city of kings. The treasuries hold five thousand talents — more silver than the world has words for. In the great hall where Xerxes planned his war on Hellas, Thais of Athens puts a torch in your hand and the army roars for the sight.

choices.text: Take the diadem: stay in the East, and rule both worlds from Persepolis
Burn the palace of Xerxes — let Hellas hear the fire from across the sea
Seal the treasuries and leave the halls standing — you are a king, not a raider

text: You send the army home under Craterus and keep the East. You wear the diadem of Cyrus, take a royal wife, and learn to rule men who measured greatness in satrapies, not spear-lengths. The Greeks grumble that you went native; the Persians grumble that you never stopped being Greek. You rule from Persepolis into old age, and the historians will argue forever whether you grew into the crown — or it into you.

Bactria, the ceiling of the world. Bessus, who called himself Great King after burning his own, melts into the hills with the Sogdian rock-nests behind him. Every column you send comes back lighter; every fortress you take spawns two more behind it. This is war without a battle-line.

choices.text: Bind the hill clans with a marriage — take Roxane of Bactria as your wife
Winter in the hills until Bessus is dragged back to you in chains

text: The monsoon has been on the land for weeks. On the far bank of the Hydaspes, Porus waits — a king nine feet tall in the telling, with two hundred elephants in the mist. Every night your campfires shift along the bank; every night his host mirrors you, awake in the rain.

choices.text: Cross the flooded river at night, miles upstream, and fall on his flank at dawn
Treat with Porus — an ally with war elephants is worth two enemies as subjects

text: The Hyphasis river, the edge of the known world. Beyond it: the Ganges, and an empire that fields elephants by the thousand. Your army has marched eleven thousand miles and stands at the water in silence. Coenus speaks for them all: king, we would follow you anywhere but home comes first. The men watch you climb the dais.

choices.text: Leap from the dais and harangue them — they wept at Troy's tenth year too
Yield to their tears; raise twelve altars to the end of the world and turn for home
Drive them on at the spear's point — the Ocean is two rivers away

text: You force the crossing, and the Ganges is real: elephants in numbers that make Porus a fond memory. But the defeat is not by the river. That night at the Hyphasis, the shield-wall closes around the royal tent the way it once closed around Philip — and the army that loved you keeps its own counsel about what happened in the dark.

Babylon, 323 BC. You have done what no man since the god-kings: the world from the Adriatic to the Indus under one seal. Nearchus has sailed the ocean; Arabia is next, then the Pillars of Heracles. But the feasts run long, the wounds run old, and a fever has come into the city with the spring.

choices.text: Rule both worlds from Babylon — the city of cities shall be the heart of empire
Dream aloud of Arabia and the Pillars of Heracles — the fever is nothing

text: The fever breaks on the ninth day. You live. Babylon becomes the capital of the world in fact as well as seal, and the generals who would have carved your empire learn instead to govern it. You grow old planning harbors and libraries and the gradual Greek-speaking of the earth. Aristotle is disappointed by none of it, which is his way of being amazed.

The fever does not break. In the palace of Nebuchadnezzar, thirty-two years old, you ask for the strongest. The generals carve the world into pieces before your body is cold — and yet: Alexandria in Egypt, Alexandria in Bactria, Alexandria on the Indus. Seventeen cities carry your name, and the name outlives the empire. They argue about you still, which is its own kind of Olympus.
